- Correct Answer (C): King Kharavela of Kalinga (1st century BCE), known from the Hathigumpha inscription, was a devout patron of Jainism who constructed residential caves for Jain monks on the Udayagiri hills.

- Chronological disparity: Milinda (Menander I) was an Indo-Greek king who ruled during the 2nd century BCE (c. 165/155–130 BCE), known from the philosophical Buddhist text 'Milindapanha' (questions posed to Buddhist monk Nagasena).
- Why Option A is incorrect: Bimbisara was the founder-ruler of the Haryanka dynasty of Magadha (6th–5th century BCE) and a personal contemporary and patron of Gautama Buddha.
- Why Option B is incorrect: Gautama Buddha lived during the 6th–5th century BCE (c. 563–483 BCE), the same era as Bimbisara and Prasenjit.
- Why Option D is incorrect: Prasenjit (Pasenadi) was the ruler of Kosala in the 6th–5th century BCE, a contemporary of both Bimbisara and the Buddha, and closely associated with Buddhist discourses.
- Often confused with: Menander I (Milinda) is sometimes confused with earlier Greek or Mauryan figures; remember that he is an Indo-Greek ruler post-dating Alexander's invasion (326 BCE) and the Mauryan Empire by roughly three centuries.

• Correct Answer (B) Dantidurga: Dantidurga (also known as Dantivarman II, r. 735–756 CE) laid the foundation of the imperial Rashtrakuta dynasty in 753 CE by overthrowing the Badami Chalukya ruler Kirtivarman II and famously performing the 'Hiranyagarbha' (golden womb) ritual at Ujjain.
• Why Option A is incorrect: Amoghavarsha I (r. 814–878 CE) was the greatest patron king of the dynasty, credited with establishing Manyakheta (Malkhed) as the capital and authoring 'Kavirajamarga', the earliest extant Kannada work on poetics.
• Why Option C is incorrect: Dhruva (r. 780–793 CE) came to power much later and was noted for initiating Rashtrakuta military intervention in North India during the Tripartite Struggle against the Palas and Gurjara-Pratiharas.
• Why Option D is incorrect: Krishna I (r. 756–774 CE) was Dantidurga's uncle and successor who consolidated the empire and carved out the monolithic rock-cut Kailash Temple (Cave 16) at Ellora.
• Often confused with: Krishna I — students frequently confuse Krishna I with the founder due to his fame in building the monolithic Kailash Temple at Ellora, whereas the actual political foundation and independence from the Chalukyas was achieved by Dantidurga.

- Why Option B is wrong: The region between the Jhelum and Chenab is the Jech Doab, which formed the core territory of King Porus (Paurava kingdom), famous for the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BCE).

- Why Option D is wrong: The area between the Ravi and Beas is the Bari Doab, which marked the easternmost reach of Alexander the Great's campaign before his troops mutinied along the Beas (Hyphasis).
- Often confused with: Pushkalavati (modern Charsadda), another prominent capital of Gandhara; it lay to the west of the Indus near the confluence of the Swat and Kabul rivers, whereas Takshashila lay east of the Indus.
